Fidelio. Ludwig van Beethoven's Fidelio, Op. 72, is his only completed opera. A German rescue opera in two acts, it tells the story of Leonore, a courageous Spanish noblewoman. To save her husband Florestan, who is being held as a political prisoner in a secret dungeon, Leonore disguises herself as a young man named Fidelio to secure a job working for the prison jailer Rocco. The opera is celebrated for its themes of political liberty, marital fidelity, and triumph over tyranny, culminating in the dramatic rescue of Florestan.

Leonore infiltrates the prison in her disguise and stands between her husband and his executioner. Florestan begins Act II with the dramatic cry "Gott! Welch Dunkel hier!"—"God! What darkness here!"—as he awakens in the deepest dungeon. Don Pizarro is the villainous governor of the prison who has secretly locked Florestan away and resolves to murder him to cover up his crimes. Rocco is the kindly, money-conscious jailer whose daughter Marzelline falls in love with Fidelio, ignoring her former suitor Jaquino.

A famous Act I choral number, the Prisoners' Chorus, titled "O welche Lust," expresses the prisoners' joy at briefly walking in the sunlight. During the climactic Act II murder attempt, a trumpet call is played offstage, signaling the arrival of the state minister Don Fernando, which halts the execution and leads to the reunion and liberation.

The overtures were a source of great struggle for Beethoven, who composed four distinct versions. Three are known as Leonore overtures, numbered one, two, and three, while the final and lighter Fidelio overture was used in the 1814 revision. The opera was first completed in 1805 and then substantially revised in 1814. Fidelio stands as Beethoven's sole contribution to the operatic repertoire, and it emerged during an era when the rescue opera genre, originating in post-Revolutionary France, reflected the period's focus on political liberation and human freedom.
